system:
You are the analysis agent of a reporting platform for Australia's threatened species. Conservation practitioners — people in government agencies, NGOs and recovery teams who decide where to survey, what to protect and what to escalate — read what you produce. You have read-only SQL access to the platform's database and produce insights from it, each grounded in queries you ran.

# The data

PostgreSQL 17 with PostGIS 3.5. The corpus is every occurrence record the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA) tags as nationally threatened (EPBC Critically Endangered, Endangered or Vulnerable), observed January 2015 to 2026-09-30, from one bulk download (DOI 10.26197/ala.40eee344-07ce-48d2-9ec2-be39574ff4c7): about 2.1 million records, 1,850 taxa, 300+ contributing datasets. Alongside it are all-taxa effort counts per 0.1° cell per month for the same period.

corpus.analysable_occurrences — VIEW — the records to analyse: occurrences that are valid, dated, and not from telemetry (animal-tracking) datasets. Includes population ('wild' or 'managed' — managed means a fenced haven, reintroduction or other managed population, set from the dataset or from corpus.managed_populations) and dataset_kind (the dataset's own kind). Prefer this over occurrences.
  columns: record_id text, source text, source_record_id text, occurrence_id text, harvest_id text, snapshot_page text, fetched_at timestamp with time zone, data_resource_uid text, license text, taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, event_date timestamp with time zone, first_loaded_at timestamp with time zone, decimal_latitude double precision, decimal_longitude double precision, coordinate_uncertainty_m double precision, state_province text, ibra_region text, locality text, geom USER-DEFINED, basis_of_record text, individual_count integer, recorded_by_pseudonym text, occurrence_remarks text, event_remarks text, source_assertions ARRAY, is_valid boolean, issue_count integer, cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, event_day date, managed_by_rule boolean, dataset_kind text, population text

corpus.datasets — TABLE — contributing datasets; kind is 'wild', 'managed' (fenced havens, reintroductions) or 'telemetry' (excluded from analysable_occurrences).
  columns: data_resource_uid text, name text, kind text, kind_reason text, first_seen_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.effort_cells — TABLE — ALL-taxa record counts (threatened or not, telemetry excluded) per 0.1° cell per month: the denominator for reporting rates. Join on cell_lat/cell_lon and month.
  columns: cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, period_start date, period_end date, records integer, harvest_id text

corpus.harvest_runs — TABLE — provenance of each harvest (the corpus download and the effort counts).
  columns: harvest_id text, harvest_key text, run_id text, source text, description text, query jsonb, started_at timestamp with time zone, finished_at timestamp with time zone, expected_records integer, retrieved_records integer, complete boolean, corpus_hash text, request_count integer, warnings jsonb, analysis jsonb, loaded_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.managed_populations — TABLE — curated rules marking managed populations: a taxon in a state (optionally narrowed to an IBRA region and a dataset), e.g. Bilby in NSW, where it survives only in fenced havens, or Woylie in AWC's Mt Gibson haven. Already applied in analysable_occurrences.population.
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, state_province text, note text, rule_id integer, ibra_region text, data_resource_uid text

corpus.occurrences — TABLE — every canonical occurrence record, telemetry included. event_date is the observation instant (timestamptz); event_day is its Australian Eastern local date. geom is a PostGIS Point (SRID 4326); cell_lat/cell_lon are the 0.1° grid cell (rounded to nearest, as ALA assigns them).
  columns: record_id text, source text, source_record_id text, occurrence_id text, harvest_id text, snapshot_page text, fetched_at timestamp with time zone, data_resource_uid text, license text, taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, event_date timestamp with time zone, first_loaded_at timestamp with time zone, decimal_latitude double precision, decimal_longitude double precision, coordinate_uncertainty_m double precision, state_province text, ibra_region text, locality text, geom USER-DEFINED, basis_of_record text, individual_count integer, recorded_by_pseudonym text, occurrence_remarks text, event_remarks text, source_assertions ARRAY, is_valid boolean, issue_count integer, cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, event_day date, managed_by_rule boolean

corpus.taxa — TABLE — one row per taxon (key taxon_concept_id); national_status is the EPBC status ALA attached.
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, taxon_rank text, kingdom text, phylum text, taxon_class text, taxon_order text, family text, genus text, national_status text, status_seen_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.taxon_tiers — VIEW — per taxon: analysable records since 2015, last_record_day, and statistical_tier (≥100 records since 2015).
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, records_since_2015 bigint, last_record_day date, statistical_tier boolean

Useful facts: EPSG:3577 (Australian Albers, equal-area, metres) is available for gridding and areas; ibra_region is the IBRA 7 bioregion (null offshore — IBRA covers land only); coordinate_uncertainty_m is the radius the true position may lie within.

**Dates: use event_day** (the Australian Eastern local date) for every date window, count by period and date you report — not event_date, which is an instant stored in UTC and would put early-morning Australian records on the previous day.

# Known properties of this data — read before interpreting anything

- **Records measure effort as much as animals.** These are mostly opportunistic records. All-taxa recording roughly doubled between 2017–19 and 2022–24 (about 1.9×), so counts and range measures grow with effort. Use corpus.effort_cells as a denominator where it matters.
- **Recent months are incomplete.** Datasets reach ALA months to a year late: January–August 2026 holds about 20% of the records January–August 2024 holds, and eBird (the largest dataset) has not loaded 2026 at all. A recent decline is not evidence of anything until this is accounted for.
- **Sources start and stop.** A compilation that ends in 2020, or a targeted survey wound up inside an ongoing state atlas, looks exactly like range loss. Check which datasets carry a taxon's records in each period before calling a change real.
- **Locations vary in precision.** About half the analysable records are located to within 2 km; about a third state no uncertainty; ALA generalises many sensitive species to roughly 10 km.
- **Managed populations** (population = 'managed': fenced havens, reintroductions) are in the analysable view and are not wild trend.
- **National status** is as ALA attached it. Never infer, change or second-guess a taxon's conservation status.
- Taxonomy can shift: a taxon "disappearing" from a region can be a name re-assignment.

# How to work

- Call run_sql with one SELECT (or WITH … SELECT) per call, no trailing statements. Results are capped at 200 rows and queries time out after 30 s, so aggregate in SQL rather than pulling rows. Each call returns a query_id.
- Record each insight with record_insight as soon as it is established. Every insight cites the query_ids whose results support it, and every number in it must be a value those queries returned or simple arithmetic on them. Do not state figures you did not query.
- taxon_concept_id must be copied exactly from corpus.taxa; when an insight is about several taxa, put the main one there (or null) and list the others in related_taxa; region is an IBRA region name exactly as in ibra_region, or null for a national insight; period_start and period_end are the window the insight describes.
- Say how confident you are and why, in the confidence field: record counts, the datasets involved, effort, precision, and any artefact that could explain the pattern.
- When you have recorded everything worth recording, stop.

tools.name: run_sql
tools.description: Run one read-only SQL query (a single SELECT or WITH … SELECT) against the corpus. Returns a query_id, the columns and up to 200 rows. Cite the query_id in any insight that relies on the result.

sql.description: One SELECT or WITH … SELECT statement.

purpose.description: One line: what this query is for.

tools.name: record_insight
tools.description: Record one insight. Every figure must come from the cited queries.

category.description: A short label of your own for the kind of insight.

taxon_concept_id.description: Exactly as in corpus.taxa, or null for a non-taxon insight.

related_taxa.description: Optional: other taxon_concept_ids this insight is about, exactly as in corpus.taxa.

region.description: IBRA region name exactly as in ibra_region, or null for national.

period_start.description: YYYY-MM-DD — start of the window the insight describes.

figures.description: The numbers behind the insight, as returned by your queries.

confidence.description: Why this should or should not be trusted: records, datasets, effort, precision, possible artefacts.

summary.description: One or two sentences a practitioner can act on.

query_ids.description: The run_sql query_ids whose results support this insight.

messages.content:
It is October 2026. A conservation practitioner responsible for Australia's threatened species asks: from this data, what should I know right now — what has changed, what is concerning, what is new, and where are we blind?

Investigate as you judge best and record each insight worth their attention — aim for the most important 20 to 40. For each, be explicit about confidence and about any data artefact that could explain the pattern.

input.sql: SELECT extract(year from event_day)::int yr, count(*) recs, count(distinct taxon_concept_id) taxa, count(distinct data_resource_uid) ds, sum((population='managed')::int) managed FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
input.purpose: Yearly overview of analysable records

input.sql: SELECT extract(year from period_start)::int yr, sum(records) recs, count(*) cellmonths FROM corpus.effort_cells GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
input.purpose: All-taxa effort by year

input.sql: SELECT national_status, count(*) taxa, sum(statistical_tier::int) stat_tier, sum((records_since_2015=0)::int) zero, sum((last_record_day < '2021-01-01')::int) none_since_2021, sum(records_since_2015) recs FROM corpus.taxon_tiers GROUP BY 1
input.purpose: Taxa by status and tier

input.sql: SELECT extract(month from event_day)::int m, sum((extract(year from event_day)=2024)::int) y2024, sum((extract(year from event_day)=2025)::int) y2025, sum((extract(year from event_day)=2026)::int) y2026 FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences WHERE event_day>='2024-01-01' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
input.purpose: Monthly completeness 2024-2026

input.sql: SELECT d.name, o.data_resource_uid, count(*) total, sum((event_day<'2020-01-01')::int) pre2020, sum((event_day>='2024-01-01' and event_day<'2025-01-01')::int) y2024, sum((event_day>='2025-01-01' and event_day<'2026-01-01')::int) y2025, sum((event_day>='2026-01-01')::int) y2026, max(event_day) last_day FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences o JOIN corpus.datasets d USING (data_resource_uid) GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 30
input.purpose: Top datasets and their temporal coverage

input.sql: SELECT state_province, count(*) recs, count(distinct taxon_concept_id) taxa, sum((event_day>='2022-01-01' and event_day<'2025-01-01')::int) y22_24, sum((event_day>='2017-01-01' and event_day<'2020-01-01')::int) y17_19, sum((population='managed')::int) managed, round(avg((coordinate_uncertainty_m<=2000)::int)::numeric,2) prec2km, round(avg((coordinate_uncertainty_m is null)::int)::numeric,2) nounc FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC
input.purpose: State coverage and precision

input.sql: WITH s AS (SELECT o.state_province, d.name, count(*) n, row_number() over (partition by o.state_province order by count(*) desc) rk FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences o JOIN corpus.datasets d USING(data_resource_uid) GROUP BY 1,2) SELECT * FROM s WHERE rk<=3 ORDER BY state_province, rk

WITH w AS (SELECT taxon_concept_id, cell_lat, cell_lon, event_day FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences WHERE population='wild' AND event_day>='2017-01-01' AND event_day<'2025-01-01' AND (event_day<'2020-01-01' OR event_day>='2022-01-01')),
cells AS (SELECT DISTINCT taxon_concept_id, cell_lat, cell_lon FROM w),
eff AS (SELECT cell_lat, cell_lon, sum(records) FILTER (WHERE period_start<'2020-01-01' AND period_start>='2017-01-01') e1, sum(records) FILTER (WHERE period_start>='2022-01-01' AND period_start<'2025-01-01') e2 FROM corpus.effort_cells GROUP BY 1,2),
te AS (SELECT c.taxon_concept_id, sum(e.e1) e1, sum(e.e2) e2, count(*) ncells FROM cells c JOIN eff e USING (cell_lat,cell_lon) GROUP BY 1),
tr AS (SELECT taxon_concept_id, count(*) FILTER (WHERE event_day<'2020-01-01') r1, count(*) FILTER (WHERE event_day>='2022-01-01') r2 FROM w GROUP BY 1)
SELECT t.taxon_concept_id, x.scientific_name, x.vernacular_name, x.national_status, tr.r1, tr.r2, te.ncells, round((tr.r2::numeric/nullif(te.e2,0))/(nullif(tr.r1,0)::numeric/nullif(te.e1,0)),2) rr_ratio
FROM tr JOIN te t USING (taxon_concept_id) JOIN corpus.taxa x USING (taxon_concept_id)
WHERE tr.r1+tr.r2>=200 ORDER BY rr_ratio ASC NULLS FIRST LIMIT 60
input.purpose: Effort-adjusted reporting-rate change 2017-19 vs 2022-24, biggest declines

WITH w AS (SELECT o.taxon_concept_id, cell_lat, cell_lon, event_day FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences o JOIN corpus.taxa x USING(taxon_concept_id) WHERE x.kingdom='Animalia' AND x.taxon_class<>'Aves' AND population='wild' AND event_day>='2017-01-01' AND event_day<'2025-01-01' AND (event_day<'2020-01-01' OR event_day>='2022-01-01')),
cells AS (SELECT DISTINCT taxon_concept_id, cell_lat, cell_lon FROM w),
eff AS (SELECT cell_lat, cell_lon, sum(records) FILTER (WHERE period_start<'2020-01-01' AND period_start>='2017-01-01') e1, sum(records) FILTER (WHERE period_start>='2022-01-01' AND period_start<'2025-01-01') e2 FROM corpus.effort_cells GROUP BY 1,2),
te AS (SELECT c.taxon_concept_id, sum(e.e1) e1, sum(e.e2) e2 FROM cells c JOIN eff e USING (cell_lat,cell_lon) GROUP BY 1),
tr AS (SELECT taxon_concept_id, count(*) FILTER (WHERE event_day<'2020-01-01') r1, count(*) FILTER (WHERE event_day>='2022-01-01') r2, count(distinct (cell_lat,cell_lon)) FILTER (WHERE event_day<'2020-01-01') c1, count(distinct (cell_lat,cell_lon)) FILTER (WHERE event_day>='2022-01-01') c2 FROM w GROUP BY 1)
SELECT tr.taxon_concept_id, x.vernacular_name, x.taxon_class, x.national_status, tr.r1, tr.r2, tr.c1, tr.c2, round((tr.r2::numeric/nullif(te.e2,0))/(nullif(tr.r1,0)::numeric/nullif(te.e1,0)),2) rr_ratio
FROM tr JOIN te USING (taxon_concept_id) JOIN corpus.taxa x USING (taxon_concept_id)
WHERE tr.r1+tr.r2>=400 AND tr.r1>0 AND tr.r2>0 ORDER BY rr_ratio LIMIT 60

confidence.reason: Direct counts from the whole analysable view. input.summary: Do not read any drop in late 2025 or 2026 as a decline. January–August 2026 holds 33,769 records, about 23% of the 148,479 for January–August 2024. eBird has nothing after August 2025, and only 31 datasets have supplied any 2026 records (58 did for 2024). confidence.reason: Effort counts come from the all-taxa effort table, which excludes telemetry. Raw threatened-record growth roughly tracks effort growth, so raw counts and range sizes inflate over time for every taxon.

input.summary: All-taxa recording effort grew about 3.2× from 2015 to 2024 (4.31M to 13.62M records), and the number of 0.1° cell-months surveyed nearly doubled. Threatened-species records tripled over the same years (87,760 to 263,234), mostly because of effort. Any raw increase in records or range is unreliable unless it is scaled by effort.

confidence.reason: Effort-scaled reporting rates for these NT mammals fall by 98–100%, but nearly all their pre-2020 records came from Fauna Atlas N.T., which has supplied almost nothing since 2021 (1 record in 2024). Only scattered iNaturalist and AWC records continue. The fall reflects the data feed stopping and is not evidence of decline in the wild.

input.summary: The Top End's threatened mammals have essentially no data in ALA since 2021. Fauna Atlas N.T. fell from 4,447 records in 2018 to 1 in 2024, and taxa such as Djintamoonga (Black-footed Tree-rat), Brush-tailed Tree-rat, Arnhem Land Rock-rat and Northern Brushtail Possum went quiet with it. Ask NT DEPWS for its recent monitoring data before reading this as decline. For these species the platform is currently blind.

confidence.level: high that this is a data artefact
confidence.reason: The Victorian Biodiversity Atlas roughly halved after 2019 and has barely loaded 2025–26. Several apparent Victorian declines are entirely VBA drop-outs, e.g. Golden Sun Moth (effort-scaled reporting rate ×0.07) and SE Red-tailed Black-cockatoo (×0.15), while BirdLife Birdata records of the cockatoo rose from 69 to 124.

input.summary: The Victorian Biodiversity Atlas has shrunk, from 21,702 threatened records in 2018 to about 11,000 a year in 2022–24 and only 2,909 in 2025. Apparent Victorian declines (Golden Sun Moth, South-eastern Red-tailed Black-cockatoo, the Victorian Regent Honeyeater records) largely track this drop. Check them against VBA directly or against independent sources before acting.

confidence.reason: State composition comes straight from the analysable view. Queensland's state wildlife database (WildNet) supplies only 5,354 records and about 60 a year since 2024, so non-bird groups in Queensland rest on iNaturalist and museums. 81% of Queensland records state no coordinate uncertainty.

input.summary: For anything other than birds, Queensland is largely blind. Its 44 threatened mammal taxa have 8,479 records in total and its 296 threatened plants 12,910, against 305,317 mammal records in NSW. WildNet contributes about 60 records a year. Do not interpret absences or trends for Queensland non-bird taxa from this platform; get WildNet data directly.

input.summary: Western Australia's data cannot support site-scale decisions: 223,387 of its 225,528 records are located only to 10–20 km. Its 321 threatened plant taxa, the largest state share, have just 2,879 records between them. WA plant status and range questions need DBCA/WAHerb data; this platform effectively sees WA birds plus AWC sanctuary monitoring.

confidence.reason: No Tasmanian government dataset (Natural Values Atlas) is among the top contributors, and 93% of Tasmanian records are birds from citizen-science sources.

input.summary: Tasmania is visible only through birdwatchers. Its 13 threatened mammal taxa have 1,789 records and its 86 threatened plants 1,000 over 11 years, almost all from eBird, Birdata and iNaturalist. Tasmanian Devil, for example, has about 100 records a year. Without the Natural Values Atlas, this platform cannot assess Tasmanian mammals, plants or invertebrates.

confidence.reason: Two independent normalisations agree: effort-scaled across all sources (×0.47) and eBird plus Birdata relative to all threatened-bird records in those sources (×0.60). input.summary: Painted Honeyeater is being reported less often relative to effort. Recorded 0.1° cells fell from 277 in 2017–19 to 204 in 2022–24, even though recording effort roughly doubled. confidence.reason: The all-source ratio (×0.19) is inflated by two sources ending (the NESP A12 compilation and WildNet). input.summary: Lesser Sand Plover (Endangered) is the clearest shorebird decline in the citizen-science data. Its share of eBird and Birdata threatened-bird records roughly halved between 2017–19 and 2022–24, and its recorded cells fell from 135 to 81. Part of the all-source drop is compilations ending, but the citizen-science signal remains. Prioritise it in shorebird count reviews.

confidence.reason: Large samples: more than 13,000 Curlew Sandpiper records in each period. Both normalisations point down. input.summary: Curlew Sandpiper (Critically Endangered) is reported about 25–50% less often relative to effort in 2022–24 than in 2017–19. Raw records were flat (13,534 to 13,266) while effort roughly doubled. Sharp-tailed Sandpiper and Latham's Snipe show similar falls of 30–50%. Eastern Curlew does not (×0.86 to ×1.02). Compare against Shorebirds 2020 counts, which measure abundance rather than presence.

Raw record counts rose, which hides the fall. Flag both for structured woodland-bird survey checks.

confidence.reason: Record counts are misleading here: they rose because birders repeatedly visit a few known flocks. The number of distinct cells is the more telling measure and it halved in the citizen-science data while effort doubled. The 2017 Victorian spike (497 records) probably reflects captive-release monitoring, which is not flagged as managed, and VBA's decline also removes Victorian records. input.summary: Regent Honeyeater (Critically Endangered) is being recorded in fewer places even as observers watch it more. In eBird and Birdata, the number of 0.1° cells with records halved from 51 in 2017–19 to 24 in 2022–24 while its records doubled, and Victorian records have almost vanished (none in 2024). Read the rising record count as concentration on known flocks, not recovery.

confidence.reason: In each case one dataset accounts for the change: Birdata uploads of a single observer pseudonym in SA and Victoria for the bittern, SA Fauna post-fire survey work for the KI Dunnart, and BioNet and SA Fauna flying-fox census uploads ending. Independent sources such as eBird NSW (bittern 214 to 191) show no comparable change.

input.summary: Several of the largest apparent changes are single programs starting or stopping, not population change. Australasian Bittern's 7.5× rise comes from Birdata uploads under one observer pseudonym in SA (63 to 6,528 records), probably targeted monitoring. Kangaroo Island Dunnart's 13.8× rise is post-fire survey effort in SA Fauna. Grey-headed Flying-fox's ×0.16 fall is census uploads to BioNet and SA Fauna tailing off. Do not report any of these as trends.

confidence.reason: These taxa drew at least 70% of their pre-2020 records from one state atlas, and that atlas's records for them fell by more than 80%. The pattern (thousands of records from a few cells, then almost none) is typical of a one-off targeted survey or monitoring project ending. A few could be genuine losses, for example after the 2019–20 fires, but this data cannot tell which.

input.summary: The steepest apparent declines in the platform mostly mark survey projects ending. Examples include Swamp Mint-bush (1,650 records to 1), Minyon Quandong (2,370 to 16) and Atlas Rainforest Ground-beetle (1,907 to 19). Before escalating any of them, ask the data custodians whether monitoring stopped. A handful may be real post-fire losses.

content.text:
I've recorded 34 insights. The short version: the steepest declines in this data mostly mark survey feeds stopping, but a handful of bird declines hold up after scaling by effort and checking sources, and large parts of the country and several key groups are effectively unmonitored here.

**Data artefacts to read every result through**
- **Recent data are incomplete.** January–August 2026 holds about 23% of the January–August 2024 records. eBird, the largest dataset, has nothing after August 2025, and the all-taxa effort denominator halves between August and September 2025. Don't compare reporting rates across that break, and treat any 2025–26 drop as a loading gap.
- **Effort tripled.** All-taxa recording grew about 3.2× from 2015 to 2024, so raw counts and range sizes rise for almost every taxon. Only effort-scaled measures mean anything.
- **Most steep "declines" are projects ending.** Of 82 taxa that depended on NSW BioNet before 2020, 58 have collapsed in the data, plus 23 SA Flora taxa. Other examples are Swamp Mint-bush, Mount Lofty Ranges Southern Emu-wren, Fleay's Frog, Gould's Petrel, Grey-headed Flying-fox and Lord Howe Pied Currawong. The big "rises" are single programs starting: Australasian Bittern (about 6,500 Birdata records under one observer pseudonym in SA) and Kangaroo Island Dunnart (post-fire surveys). Ask the custodians before escalating any of these.

**Concerning: bird declines that hold up across sources**
These are confirmed two ways: scaled by all-taxa effort, and as a share of threatened-bird records within eBird and Birdata alone, year by year. The second measure isn't affected by datasets starting or stopping.
- **Lesser Sand Plover:** share fell from 19.2 to 3.1 per 10,000 records (2015–2024); recorded cells fell from 135 to 81.
- **Australian Fairy Tern:** share roughly halved since 2018; worst in WA (×0.39).
- **Curlew Sandpiper (Critically Endangered):** reported 25–50% less often relative to effort; worst in SA and Tasmania. Sharp-tailed Sandpiper and Latham's Snipe show similar falls; Eastern Curlew does not.
- **Woodland birds:** South-eastern Brown Treecreeper (worst in Qld and NSW) and South-eastern Hooded Robin (worst in NSW) are down about 35–40%, while Southern Whiteface and Superb Parrot are steady.
- **Painted Honeyeater:** down by both measures; it fluctuates year to year but stays below its 2017–19 level.
- **Regent Honeyeater (Critically Endangered):** records doubled, but the number of recorded cells halved (51 to 24) and Victorian records have almost gone. That pattern points to observers concentrating on known flocks, not recovery.

These are presence records, not counts, so treat them as leads to check against structured surveys and shorebird counts.

**No decline signal, or cautious good news**
- Gang-gang Cockatoo and Southern Greater Glider are flat relative to effort.
- Swift Parrot is slightly down, with a stable footprint.
- Malleefowl and the Brush-tailed and Yellow-footed Rock-wallabies are reported more often, though much of that is targeted monitoring.

**New**
- 249 taxa have no records before 2021; 64 first appear in 2024 or later, mostly newly listed or newly described plants.
- Lax Leek-orchid (Critically Endangered) first appeared on 23 Sep 2026.
- Canberra Grassland Earless Dragon records now come from NSW (133 in 2025–26), as ACT monitoring data have largely stopped arriving.
- Some 2025–26 records fall outside a taxon's known bioregions and need vetting before anyone treats them as range extensions, notably 8 eBird Red Goshawk records in the Great Sandy Desert.

**Where we're blind**
- **Northern Territory:** the Fauna Atlas fell from about 4,400 records in 2018 to 1 in 2024, so Top End mammals have essentially no data since 2021. Northern dolphins, sawfish and Pacific Ridley turtle lost every source when their survey compilations ended around 2020.
- **Other states:**
  - Queensland non-birds rest on about 60 state-database records a year.
  - Almost all Western Australian records are only located to 10–20 km, and its 321 threatened plants have 2,879 records between them.
  - Tasmania is visible only through birdwatchers.
  - The Victorian state atlas has shrunk sharply since 2019.
- **Specific taxa and groups:**
  - **Koala:** the listed population has just 8 records, because ordinary sightings are never tagged as the threatened population.
  - **Fenced havens:** Bilby, Woylie and Central Rock-rat records are almost all from havens, with wild populations barely recorded.
  - **Frogs:** the FrogID feed stops in November 2024.
  - **Islands:** island endemics are thinly covered.
  - **Arid interior:** inland bioregions have almost no records.
- **Too few records for trends:** only 86 of 392 Critically Endangered taxa have enough records (100 or more) for any trend estimate. 21 Critically Endangered animals and 57 Critically Endangered plants have no record since 2021, including Coxen's Fig-parrot and Baw Baw Frog. Ask the recovery teams whether data exist; if not, these are survey priorities.
- **Location precision:** 57% of bird records give no uncertainty, and of those that do, 48% are uncertain by 10 km or more. That rules out site-scale use without unobscured data from the custodians.

**Provenance:** the corpus download is complete (2,108,546 records), but ALA didn't confirm its DOI. Check that before citing it in a report.
